  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A has sourced evidence that people already pay in this category. Expiration Reminder ($49-$349/mo), RenewalTracker ($49/mo) and ClearBot ($500-$800/location/yr) all publish real pricing. Idea B's price anchors come from Nalvis, which is pre-launch and waitlist-only, and Since.dev's $149 Studio tier. Neither brief shows anyone actually paying in B's category.",
    "Idea B faces heavy price pressure from free tools. Nalvis's core engine, mendapi (AGPL) and ApiPatch are all open source. Idea A's competitors charge money, and the brief lists none that give the product away.",
    "Idea B has a trust barrier that blocks a first sale within 90 days. Customers must grant PR and write access to their code, and B's own brief says SOC 2 Type II is commonly expected and likely out of scope for a 6-week build. Idea A's liability risk is real but narrower. The brief frames it as a legal-review question, not a certification requirement.",
    "Idea A has a buildable narrow version. The brief says baseline deadline tracking, alerts and a dashboard are buildable in six weeks by one person with AI agents, matching the cheapest paid competitors. That lets a solo operator skip the risky 50-state rule-change monitoring at first.",
    "Idea A's demand evidence comes from practitioners in three separate communities: a structural engineer, a therapist and small-business owners. Two of Idea B's three demand quotes come from dev.to authors whose post titles or content point to monitoring or fix approaches, so they may be promoting a solution rather than purely reporting pain."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's price hypothesis ($14-150/mo) rests on Nalvis's $14/mo hosted tier, which the brief itself describes as pre-launch/waitlist, and Since.dev's $149 Studio tier. Neither comes with any evidence of paying customers. With free, open-source engines available, the brief contains no proof that this category can charge at all. B's claim that vendors like Stripe are building native tooling also has no citation, so it counts as unsourced.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. Idea A has real weaknesses. Its paid-acquisition figures ($87-200 CPL) come from what the brief calls an AI-aggregated marketing blog. Its affiliate data is only an adjacent-market proxy. Its own demand evidence shows buyers sticking with spreadsheets, which could make converting them to paid hard. Both markets look crowded. A wins mainly because its brief shows a proven paying market, while B's shows free competitors and a steep trust requirement. It does not win because A's go-to-market is validated."
}
